title: Possession of Crystal Meth (Mutoriro)
description: A 22‑year‑old university student is found in possession of 5 grams of crystal methamphetamine (known locally as Mutoriro or Guka) during a police raid on a nightclub. He admits to using the drug occasionally and claims it was for personal use.
options: Level 10 fine or up to 10 years imprisonment (Section 157)
Level 14 fine and mandatory 15–20 years imprisonment (Section 156)
Release with a warning and community service
Fine only, no imprisonment
statute: Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act [Chapter 9:23], Section 157
penalty: Fine up to Level 10, imprisonment not exceeding 10 years, or both.
takeaway: Unlawful possession of dangerous drugs like crystal meth is prosecuted under Section 157, which provides for a fine and/or up to 10 years in prison. Aggravated dealing (Section 156) applies to larger‑scale trafficking and carries 15–20 years.

title: Aggravated Dealing in Cocaine
description: A drug syndicate leader is arrested with 2 kg of cocaine and several firearms. He is found to be operating an organised network that recruited minors to act as couriers. He is charged under the aggravated dealing provisions.
options: Fine up to Level 14 and 10 years imprisonment
Mandatory imprisonment of 15 to 20 years (Section 156 aggravated)
5 years imprisonment and fine
Deportation and fine
statute: Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act [Chapter 9:23], Section 156 (Aggravated Circumstances)
penalty: Imprisonment for 15 to 20 years, plus a fine not below Level 14.
takeaway: Aggravated dealing includes organised crime, use of violence, enticement of minors, or repeat offenses. The mandatory minimum is 15 years' imprisonment, reflecting the severity of the offense.

title: Smuggling Codeine Syrup (Broncleer)
description: A pharmacist is caught importing 500 bottles of codeine‑based cough syrup (Broncleer) without a Medicines Control Authority of Zimbabwe (MCAZ) licence. The bottles lack proper registration and are destined for illegal sale on the black market.
options: Seizure of goods and a fine under MASCA
Up to 5 years imprisonment and a fine (MASCA Section 100)
10 years imprisonment under the Dangerous Drugs Act
No offence, as codeine is a legal medicine
statute: Medicines and Allied Substances Control Act (MASCA) [Chapter 15:03], Section 38/100
penalty: Fine up to Level 12, confiscation, and imprisonment up to 5 to 10 years.
takeaway: Unlawful importation or dealing in prescription‑only medicines like codeine is prosecuted under MASCA, with penalties including imprisonment and substantial fines. Broncleer is a controlled substance when imported without approval.

title: Unlicensed Brewing of Illicit Spirits (Kachasu)
description: A rural community member is found operating a large‑scale distillery producing high‑proof spirits (Kachasu / Musombodia) without a licence. The operation poses a public health risk due to potential methanol contamination.
options: Fines up to Level 7 and up to 2 years imprisonment (Liquor Act)
Immediate destruction of equipment and a warning
10 years imprisonment under the Dangerous Drugs Act
No offence, as traditional brewing is protected
statute: Liquor Act [Chapter 14:12] and Harmful Liquids Act [Chapter 14:10]
penalty: Fines up to Level 7, forfeiture/destruction of equipment, and imprisonment up to 1 to 2 years.
takeaway: Illicit distillation is a serious regulatory offence because of health risks and revenue loss. Penalties include fines and jail time, and courts typically order destruction of the brewing apparatus.

title: Unauthorised Cultivation of Cannabis (Mbanje)
description: A small‑scale farmer is growing 200 cannabis plants on his land without a medical or industrial hemp licence. He claims the cannabis is for his own traditional use and not for sale.
options: Fine up to Level 10 or imprisonment up to 10 years (Section 158)
Mandatory 15 years under Section 156 (dealing)
6 months imprisonment only
Legal if for personal use
statute: Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act [Chapter 9:23], Section 158
penalty: A fine up to Level 10, imprisonment not exceeding 10 years, or both.
takeaway: Unlawful cultivation of cannabis is dealt with under Section 158, with penalties comparable to possession. Commercial cultivation may be charged as dealing under Section 156, attracting harsher sentences.

title: Retail of Solvents to Minors
description: A hardware store owner sells glue, thinners, and petrol to a group of 14‑year‑olds, knowing they intend to inhale the fumes for intoxication. The minors later suffer severe health effects.
options: Fines or up to 2 years imprisonment (Children's Act)
5 years imprisonment under the Dangerous Drugs Act
No offence, as solvents are legal products
Only a warning and a small fine
statute: Children's Act [Chapter 5:06] and Criminal Law (Public Nuisance)
penalty: Fines or imprisonment up to 2 years for endangering a minor.
takeaway: While solvent inhalation is not a drug offense per se, retailers who supply these substances to minors for intoxication can be prosecuted under the Children's Act for endangering the welfare of a child.

title: Unlicensed Forex & Crypto Trading Scheme
description: A self‑styled investment guru runs a forex/crypto trading scheme, promising guaranteed monthly returns. He operates without a licence from the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, and the scheme shows hallmarks of a ponzi structure. Investors lose their funds.
options: Imprisonment up to 10–14 years and forfeiture (Exchange Control Act & Fraud)
2 years imprisonment only
Civil lawsuit only, no criminal liability
Fine up to Level 6
statute: Exchange Control Act [Chapter 22:05] and Criminal Law Code (Fraud, Section 136)
penalty: Imprisonment up to 10 to 14 years and mandatory forfeiture of illicit funds.
takeaway: Unlicensed foreign currency dealing and fraudulent investment schemes are taken seriously, with penalties comparable to fraud and financial crimes. Courts often order restitution and forfeiture.

title: Operating an Illegal Gambling Parlour
description: A businessman is running an unlicensed slot machine arcade in a shopping centre, offering gambling without a permit from the Lotteries and Gaming Board. The machines are not registered.
options: Fines up to Level 10 and up to 2 years imprisonment (Lotteries and Gaming Act)
10 years imprisonment under the Criminal Law Code
Seizure of machines and a warning only
No offence, as gambling is legal in Zimbabwe
penalty: Fines up to Level 10, forfeiture of gaming machines, and up to 2 years imprisonment.
takeaway: Gambling is legal only through licensed operators. Unlicensed operations attract substantial fines, forfeiture of equipment, and jail time, reflecting the state's interest in regulating gaming activities.
